meta.title: The carbon price
meta.subtitle: How a price on emissions reaches a household bill — and why it moves the electricity price more than the gas price.
meta.one_line: Emitting carbon in GB power generation costs money, through the UK Emissions Trading Scheme and a top-up. That cost is a marginal cost to a gas generator, so it enters the electricity price through the merit order — which means it can raise the price of electricity a household uses even when that electricity came from wind.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Everything on this page is a published feature of the GB energy market, readable by anyone — so it is readable by the simulated company too, the same way a real supplier reads the codes. Nothing here is an internal of the simulation.

claim_freshness.source: HMRC/GOV.UK Climate Change Levy rate publications (CPS rates frozen since 2016 at 0.331p/kWh gas, 5.28p/kg LPG, 1.5479p/GJ solid fuels, running to 31 March 2028 at a level equivalent to £18/tCO2); published CCGT emissions-intensity estimates (approx. 320-353 kgCO2/MWh).
claim_freshness.route: Body feed read directly and each assertion checked against the published source. The pages are JS-rendered and the static HTML holds no claims, so no page was rendered at any point.
claim_freshness.found: ONE MATERIAL CORRECTION, and it is a correction this project had already made once and then lost. On 2026-08-19 (bedb08ea4) the PREDECESSOR carbon page was corrected for calling Carbon Price Support 'a tax per tonne'; on 2026-08-24 this body was written fresh to replace a stub and led with 'A carbon price is a cost per tonne emitted', naming the top-up without ever saying what it is charged on. The correction did not survive the body moving house. It is made again here, in the reader's view rather than only in metadata, with the rates and their statutory expiry. SECOND FINDING: the page's blanket refusal to carry any number was itself wrong for CPS, which is frozen and legislated rather than traded. CONFIRMED UNCHANGED: the 0.35 tCO2/MWh CCGT intensity and the ~0.35 GBP/MWh per GBP/tonne pass-through slope that rests on it.

meta.no_current_level: This page carries no current UK ETS allowance price, and that refusal is right: UKAs trade continuously and any figure written here would be wrong within weeks and read as current. The blanket version of that refusal was WRONG for the other half of the stack. CPS rates are not a traded level -- they were frozen in 2016 and are legislated unchanged to 31 March 2028 -- so refusing to state them withheld a stable, published fact and left the reader with only the per-tonne framing that this page previously got wrong. The rates are now stated in the plain rung with their expiry, which is what dates them honestly.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Great Britain prices carbon in power generation through TWO instruments, and only one of them is charged per tonne: UK ETS allowances, which a generator surrenders per tonne it emits, and Carbon Price Support, which is levied per unit of FUEL BURNED at a rate calibrated to a target price per tonne. Either way it is a marginal cost of running a gas plant, so it moves the electricity price in every hour a gas plant is setting that price — and it reaches households through the unit rate, not as a visible line.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Two things carry a carbon cost in GB power. The first is allowances under the UK Emissions Trading Scheme, which generators must surrender for what they emit — a cost per tonne of CO2, at a price set by a market that trades continuously.

The second is Carbon Price Support, a domestic top-up, and it is not charged the same way. CPS is not a tax per tonne: its rates sit inside the Climate Change Levy and fuel duty and are levied PER UNIT OF FUEL supplied for generation — 0.331p per kWh of gas, 5.28p per kg of LPG, 1.5479p per GJ of coal and other solid fuels. Those rates were frozen in 2016 and run unchanged to 31 March 2028, at a level HM Treasury calibrates to about £18 per tonne of CO2. This matters practically: if you go looking for the CPS rate you will find it quoted per unit of fuel, and a page that told you to expect a per-tonne figure has sent you to the wrong table.

For a gas generator both are a per-MWh cost like fuel is: burn gas, emit CO2, pay. So they shift that plant's position in the merit order and, when that plant is marginal, they shift the price everyone is paid.

The counter-intuitive part follows from that. Because the marginal plant sets the price for all generation, a carbon price raises the revenue of the zero-carbon plant too. A wind farm earns more because gas got more expensive. That is not a loophole — it is the mechanism working: it is what makes low-carbon generation more profitable and high-carbon generation less, which is the point.

For the household, none of this appears as a carbon line. It arrives inside the unit rate, having passed through the wholesale price.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
**The two instruments have different bases, and that is not a technicality.** UK ETS is per tonne emitted, so its burden on a plant depends on that plant's actual emissions. CPS is per unit of fuel, so its burden depends on fuel throughput, and the per-tonne equivalence is an arithmetic result of the fuel's carbon content rather than something the charge measures. The two coincide closely for a given fuel; they do not for a plant that abates.

**The cost per MWh depends on the plant's emissions intensity.** A modern CCGT emits roughly 0.35 tonnes of CO2 per MWh of electricity — published estimates for efficient plant run about 320 to 353 kg/MWh — and an old coal plant emitted far more. So a carbon price hits coal several times harder than gas per unit of output, which is precisely why a carbon price reorders the merit order rather than just raising everything.

**It enters the electricity price conditionally.** In an hour where gas is marginal, the carbon cost of that gas plant is in the price. In an hour where the margin is met without fossil generation, it largely is not.

**On the gas bill it is much smaller.** Domestic gas burned in a boiler is not in the ETS in the way generation is, and CPS rates apply only to fuel supplied for generation — so a household's gas unit rate does not carry the same pass-through. This asymmetry — carbon reaching electricity harder than gas — has a consequence people find surprising: it can make electrifying heat look worse on a bill comparison than it is on emissions.

**Levies are a separate thing.** Renewables Obligation and Contracts for Difference costs also appear on bills and are also climate policy, but they are not carbon prices — they are support schemes recovered per unit. Conflating them is the most common error here.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
**Carbon price moves should propagate into power prices with a slope near the marginal plant's emissions intensity** — roughly 0.35 £/MWh per £/tonne for CCGT — and only in the hours that plant is marginal.

**The propagation should weaken as renewable penetration rises,** because the share of hours with a fossil plant on the margin falls. A carbon price and a decarbonising grid interact: the same carbon price does less to the average electricity price each year.

**Household gas unit rates should show no comparable sensitivity,** which is the asymmetry above and is checkable directly against published rates.

live_evidence.heading: What this simulation actually does
live_evidence.body:
The simulation carries a carbon ledger and the policy-cost stack that reaches a household bill, with RO and CfD levies in the settlement records as their own lines rather than folded into an aggregate.

Explore's first stage breaks a household's unit rate into energy, network, policy and levies, and standing charge — so a reader can see how much of what they pay is not energy at all.

residuals.heading: What this page does not settle
residuals.body:
Whether the current arrangements price carbon at the right level is a policy question and this page takes no position on it.

Nor does it settle how much of the pass-through is competed away versus retained. The simulation passes wholesale cost through to the tariff by an explicit mechanism, and that mechanism is a modelling choice rather than an observed fact about the retail market.

scope_delta.heading: Where the simulation stops
scope_delta.body: No ETS allowance market: the carbon cost arrives as a published input, not as a market the company or the generators trade in. No free allocation modelling. No border adjustment. The carbon ledger accounts for emissions attributable to the book; it does not model the generator's own compliance position.
